headline: It is always worth keeping in mind that not every piece of information published by Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR) is necessarily accurate by default. Intelligence can be incomplete, outdated, or even deliberately misleading. This may be the case with the reported production of the jet-powered Geran-3 loitering munition. According to a recent GUR update, production of the Geran-3 has either been halted or is expected to be halted, with the system being replaced by the Geran-4. For some general context, the Geran-3 is essentially based on the Geran-2/Shahed-136 airframe, with little to no significant change to the overall design. The main difference is its propulsion system. The Geran-3 uses a Telefly JT80 turbojet engine, giving it a speed of approximately 300–370 km/h and a range of up to 1,000 km. It is also important not to confuse the Geran-3 with Iran’s Shahed-238. They are two different designs. The Geran-3 retains the same basic airframe and configuration as the Geran-2, with the primary change being the replacement of the piston engine with a turbojet engine. The Geran-3 appears to have served as a transitional design toward the Geran-4, which was purpose-built around the Telefly LX-WP-160 engine. The Geran-4 weighs approximately 450 kg, has broadly similar dimensions, and is reportedly valued at around $170,000–$200,000. There were also significant structural changes to the Geran-4. Unlike the Geran-2 and Geran-3, it uses a redesigned, molded one-piece fuselage intended to withstand the higher G-forces associated with high-speed flight and active maneuvering. Its propulsion system also represents a major step up in performance. With the Telefly LX-WP-160 / TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, the Geran-4's speed increases substantially, from roughly 150–185 km/h for the conventional Geran configuration to approximately 350–500 km/h.

headline: Deputy Chief of the Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR) of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, stated in an interview with RBC-Ukraine that in July 2026, the Russian Armed Forces used 153 cruise missiles against Ukraine (Kh-101, Kalibr, and Kh-32) and 198 ballistic and hypersonic missiles (Iskander-M, RM-48U, and 3M22 Zircon). The latter figure is a record. According to Skibitskyi, as of August 3, Russia had already fulfilled its annual production plan for Zircon and Oniks missiles set out in the state defense procurement order, producing 33 Zircon missiles and 60 Oniks missiles since the beginning of the year. At the same time, a modernized version of the Oniks is being produced that can engage ground targets (apparently through modifications to its active radar homing head). It also has an increased range and a larger warhead. He also stated that, overall, monthly production targets for the main types of missile weapons in Russia are currently being fulfilled at a rate of 110–120%. According to GUR data, the July production target for Kh-101 cruise missiles was fulfilled at 140%, for Kalibr cruise missiles at 111%, and for Kh-35 cruise missiles at 200%. The August production target for Kh-101 missiles is 72 units. The July target was the same, but Russia produced more, manufacturing 87 missiles. For 3M14 Kalibr missiles, the August target is 26 units. The July target was also 26, while 29 were actually produced. According to GUR data, as of August 5, the Russian Armed Forces had a stockpile of approximately 130 9M723 tactical ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system. The planned monthly production figure for these missiles is 60 units, although 65 were produced in July. According to Skibitskyi, Russia has been able to increase ballistic missile production partly by halting production of Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles and Kh-32 air-launched missiles since April. “Accordingly, the missile propellant is now going not to the Kinzhal, but to other ballistic missiles.” In addition, Russia has established production of the RM-48U quasi-ballistic missile for launch from S-400 air defense system launchers. According to Skibitskyi, the August production target for these missiles is approximately 40 units, while their estimated stockpile is around 400. Skibitskyi stated that in July, Russia somewhat reduced the intensity of its strikes against Ukraine using loitering munitions and reduced their production volumes, as Russian production is being reconfigured with an emphasis on turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 systems. In one of the recent attacks, turbojet-powered munitions already accounted for 50% of the total. At the same time, according to Skibitskyi, production of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 is currently completely dependent on supplies of turbojet engines from China, and these engines are expensive, with each costing approximately $35,000–$40,000. According to Skibitskyi, the Russian defense industry’s planned production target for strike UAVs in August this year, including the Geran-1, Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4, Geran-5, Garpiya-A1/3, Gerbera, Gerbera-Kamikaze, and Gerbera-1 types, is 11,000 units. Skibitskyi also said: “Moscow is introducing Rassvet, essentially a Russian analogue of Starlink. And they have begun deploying it much faster than anticipated in their plans. In March 2026, Russia had already placed 16 satellites into low Earth orbit. More will be launched to create a constellation totaling 292 satellites in 2027 and increase it to 924 satellites by 2035. For now, they can operate only intermittently, when a satellite passes over our territory. Once the Russians deploy a full satellite constellation, this system will operate like Starlink. A discussion is already underway about how to counter it.” It should be noted that Skibitskyi’s claim that the Rassvet system is allegedly being deployed “much faster than anticipated in their plans” is an obvious exaggeration. According to known Russian plans, six launches of carrier rockets carrying Rassvet system satellites were expected to take place in 2026, which itself appears unrealistic.

headline: New reporting sheds more light on why Trump was secretly removed from Air Force One in Ankara last month. U.S. intelligence reportedly picked up multiple streams of information indicating a specific surface to air missile threat against the aircraft carrying Trump. Someone near the NATO summit was also reportedly observed with a shoulder-fired missile. Even more concerning is that U.S. officials say Iranian intelligence knew where Trump was staying in Ankara, including the floor of the building. The threat was considered credible enough to trigger an extraordinary deception. Trump publicly boarded the legacy VC-25A 'Air Force One', was secretly removed in a catering container, and departed Turkey aboard a C-32A. The VC-25A then flew on with senior officials, staff and reporters aboard, creating the appearance that Trump was still onboard. There is no public evidence Iran actually attempted to attack the aircraft. But the combination of a potential missile threat and highly specific knowledge of Trump's location was apparently serious enough for the U.S. to treat the threat as real. The biggest unanswered question may be how Iran obtained such detailed information about the president's movements and lodging.

headline: According to the New York Times, the threat in Ankara was considered serious enough for the Secret Service to secretly move Trump off Air Force One in a catering container and onto another military aircraft. Air Force One then departed for Britain with senior officials, military personnel and journalists aboard, while those passengers were apparently unaware that the presidential aircraft itself was considered at risk. The operation was intended to conceal Trump's movements and prevent an adversary from knowing which aircraft he was actually aboard. The unusual aspect is that the deception potentially shifted the risk from the president to other passengers without their knowledge. The article also notes that this differs from previous presidential deception operations. During Bill Clinton's 1999/2000 Pakistan trip, for example, journalists were at least partially informed of the deception, and the details were publicly disclosed after the president was safe. The White House has defended the decision, with Trump saying he followed Secret Service advice. Former officials interviewed by the NYT are divided: some argue that protecting the president necessarily takes precedence, while others contend that knowingly placing uninformed civilians in a potentially targeted aircraft crosses an important line.

headline: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) says U.S. forces disabled the Panama flagged M/V VELA NOVA today after the vessel allegedly attempted to violate the U.S. naval blockade of Iran by sailing toward an Iranian port. CENTCOM says a U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the vessel's engine room, disabling its steering gear after the crew allegedly ignored repeated warnings. No injuries have been reported among the vessel's 17 crew members. The circumstances surrounding the vessel's alleged destination are less clear from publicly available AIS data. http://MarineTraffic.com data showed the VELA NOVA's stated destination as Port Jebel Ali in the United Arab Emirates, rather than an Iranian port. At the time reporting of the incident emerged, its reported position also appeared to be west of the previously established U.S. blockade line at the entrance to the Gulf of Oman. This does not necessarily contradict CENTCOM's account as AIS destination data is user entered and the U.S. military likely has intelligence not publicly available. The strike brings CENTCOM's reported totals to 55 commercial vessels redirected, two boarded and three disabled since the current blockade was established.

headline: Iran is adapting its tactics to wear down U.S. air defenses, and exploit dwindling interceptor stocks, according to new reporting from The New York Times. During five days of attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan last month, Iran combined drones with maneuvering ballistic missiles to overwhelm defensive systems. On July 17, one missile penetrated the defenses at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, killing 3 U.S. soldiers and wounding more than 100. The scale of the expenditure is becoming increasingly important: the U.S. has fired more than 1,500 Patriot interceptors during the war and reportedly has fewer than 1,700 remaining, while producing only about 600 Patriots in all of 2025. On one day during the Jordan attacks, U.S. forces reportedly fired around 50 Patriots, at roughly $4 million each. Iran has also demonstrated other adaptations, including using drones to provide targeting data that helped shoot down a U.S. F-15E in April and expanding attacks through partners such as the Houthis to force U.S. forces to defend against threats from multiple directions. The Pentagon continues to publicly deny that the U.S. has a munitions shortage.

headline: A telecom failure contributed to last week’s near-miss between Marine One and a departing passenger jet at Reagan National Airport, prompting Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to work with the FAA and White House on a fix. The incident is especially significant because mixed helicopter and commercial jet traffic around Reagan was restricted after the January 2025 midair collision that killed 67 people. Duffy said the problem involved communications systems and has now been “elevated” for action. The FAA is already spending billions to replace aging air-traffic-control telecommunications and radar infrastructure following a series of outages and failures.

headline: President Donald Trump has announced the release of former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who has been imprisoned in Russia since 2022, saying the decision came after his discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Gilman was originally sentenced to 4 1/2 years after being convicted of assaulting a Russian police officer, but his sentence was later extended after additional allegations involving prison officials. His family and U.S. advocates have disputed aspects of the case. His release comes after serious deterioration in his health. Recent reports said Gilman had been hospitalized and had spent weeks in a dissociative state, prompting increased pressure from U.S. officials for Moscow to release him on humanitarian grounds. According to Trump, Russia released Gilman without a prisoner exchange or other concessions, describing it as a humanitarian decision following his discussions with Putin. U.S. officials likewise characterized the release as a goodwill gesture rather than a negotiated swap. Gilman is now returning to the United States for medical treatment.
